images.caption:
Enap Refinerías S.A. has a storage capacity of 4,800 cubic meters, the Vinapu terminal ensures the supply of fuel to the island.
Oil comes from ships anchored off shore through of a 20.32 cm (8in) pipeline, 800 meters (2,625 ft) long. The oil is stored in 6 tanks, each holding 800 cubic meters (211,337.64 Gallons). 

There is a truck loading system (pumping room and filling platform) and a fire-fighting system. The company hast a fleet of three tanker trucks and two semi-trailers.

images.caption:
Further up the coast is this moai and it was a place where the ariki, or kings, resided temporarily, Hanga Kio’e. 
Hanga Kio’e means “Bay of the Mouse”, the name comes from an old legend about a widow who came to the cove with a mouse in the mouth, to mourn the death of her husband, his remains were buried here after the ahu (ceremonial platform) was built.

The moai that is on the Ahu Akapu has a height of 4 meters (13.1ft).

images.filename: Habitans de L'ile de Pasques by Louis Choris (British Museum, Oc2006,Prt.62).jpg
images.caption:
Habitans de l'île de Pasques: 
Print. Portrait of a man and a woman, inhabitants of Easter Island. A woman, on the left, wears a cloth wrap skirt. The man, on the right, has tattoo markings on his face, arms and legs and wears a cloth cloak, and plant leaf loin cover, and plant leaf hair ornament. Banana plant in the background. 1822.
Lithograph, printed in borwn, yellow and green tones
Print made by: Ludwig Choris; Printed by: Langlumé.
Published in: Choris, Louis (1822) "Voyage pittoresque autour du monde: avec des portraits de sauvages s'Amerique, d'Asie, a'Afrique, et des iles du Grand Ocean/ des paysages, des vues maritimes, et plusieurs objets d'histoire naturelle".

It is believed that this print was bound together (see holes on side and/or top of print) alongside other prints by Louis Choris, which are now part of the BM Pictorial Collection.

images.caption: Statues on Easter Island, 18th-century engraving. Discovered in 1721 by the Dutchman Jacob Roggeveen, monumental statues set into the earth on Easter Island seem to symbolize a secret of eternity. To this day, the wooden tablets and the stones, with over five hundred different signs carved by the same hands that erected the statues, remain unintelligible. — Illustration in the book Writing: The Story of Alphabets and Scripts (p. 127) by Georges Jean, translated by Jenny Oates, “Abrams Discoveries” series, 1992. New York: Harry N. Abrams. Description on page 202.

images.filename: Pu o Hiro (Trumpet of Hiro) in Easter Island 2018.jpg
images.caption: Pu o Hiro (translation: Trumpet of Hiro) is an ancient stone aerophone (1.25 meters high) on the northern coast of Easter Island (aka Isla de Pascua, Rapa Nui). It has small fertility symbols and holes. It was used as a musical instrument in fertility rituals by the Rapa Nui inhabitants. By blowing through the main hole it creates a deep, trumpeting sound to invoke Hiro, the god of rain in Polynesian mythology.
images.alt: Pu o Hiro (translation: Trumpet of Hiro) is an ancient stone aerophone (1.25 meters high) on the northern coast of Easter Island (aka Isla de Pascua, Rapa Nui). It has small fertility symbols and holes. It was used as a musical instrument in fertility rituals by the Rapa Nui inhabitants.
